rows.stem: Auto oxidation of chloroform in air and sunlight produces a poisonous gas known as
rows.solution:
The gas is PHOSGENE, \(\mathrm{COCl_2}\).

Chloroform is slowly oxidised by air in the presence of sunlight:
\(2\mathrm{CHCl_3} + \mathrm{O_2} \xrightarrow{\text{light}} 2\mathrm{COCl_2} + 2\mathrm{HCl}\)

Phosgene, carbonyl chloride, is extremely poisonous — it was used as a war gas — which is why chloroform is stored in DARK bottles filled nearly to the top and closed tightly: the dark excludes the light and the full bottle excludes the air, and each blocks one of the two requirements. About 1% ethanol is added as well, converting any phosgene formed into harmless diethyl carbonate.

Of the distractors, mustard gas and tear gas are quite different compounds, and chlorine is not a product of this oxidation.

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: Which of the following ligands is an ambidentate ligand ?
rows.solution:
The AMBIDENTATE ligand is the nitrite, \(\mathrm{NO_2^-}\).

An ambidentate ligand has TWO DIFFERENT DONOR ATOMS but binds the metal through only ONE at a time. The nitrite ion offers a nitrogen and two oxygens: bound through NITROGEN it is named nitro-N, through an OXYGEN nitrito-O. The two give genuinely different compounds with different colours — an instance of LINKAGE isomerism.

The other three each have a single kind of donor atom and so no choice to make: carbon monoxide donates through its carbon, ammonia through its nitrogen, water through its oxygen.

Note that ambidentate is not the same as BIDENTATE, which uses two donor atoms AT ONCE and closes a chelate ring.

rows.stem: Among the following, which has the highest value of \(\mathrm{p^Kb}\) ?
rows.solution:
The highest \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) — meaning the WEAKEST base — belongs to p-NITROANILINE.

Basicity depends on how available the nitrogen's lone pair is to accept a proton, and a substituent on the ring alters that.

The NITRO group is strongly electron WITHDRAWING, and from the PARA position it can draw the lone pair right onto its own oxygen by resonance as well as pulling inductively. A lone pair committed elsewhere is unavailable, so p-nitroaniline is much the weakest base here — \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) about 13.

The others rank the other way. Aniline is next at about 9.4; p-toluidine's methyl group RELEASES density and makes it slightly stronger. And BENZYLAMINE is the strongest of all, because its nitrogen sits one carbon away from the ring, so no delocalisation reaches it and it behaves as an ordinary aliphatic amine.

rows.stem: The slope in the plot of \(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_\mathrm{o}}{[\mathrm{R}]}\) vs. time for a first order reaction is
rows.solution:
The slope is \(+\dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\).

For a first order reaction the integrated rate equation is
\(k = \dfrac{2{\cdot}303}{t}\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]}\)

Rearranged into the form of the plotted line,
\(\log\dfrac{[\mathrm{R}]_0}{[\mathrm{R}]} = \dfrac{k}{2{\cdot}303}\,t\)

so the slope is \(k/2{\cdot}303\), it is POSITIVE, and there is no intercept — the line passes through the origin.

The sign is what this question turns on. The concentration term here is INVERTED, \([\mathrm{R}]_0\) over \([\mathrm{R}]\), so the ratio GROWS as the reaction proceeds and the line rises. Had the plot been \(\log[\mathrm{R}]\) against \(t\) the line would fall and the slope would be \(-k/2{\cdot}303\).

rows.stem: When D-glucose reacts with HI, it forms
rows.solution:
D-Glucose with hydrogen iodide gives N-HEXANE.

Prolonged heating with hydrogen iodide and red phosphorus strips EVERY oxygen out of the molecule, reducing it to the parent hydrocarbon:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow[\Delta]{\mathrm{HI}} \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_2CH_3}\)

The product is a STRAIGHT chain of six carbons, and that result is one of the classic proofs of glucose's structure: it shows the six carbons are joined in an UNBRANCHED chain, since a branched skeleton would have given a branched hexane.

The other options come from oxidations, not reductions: bromine water gives gluconic acid and concentrated nitric acid gives saccharic acid.

INVERSION of configuration occurs in the \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction.

In \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) the nucleophile attacks from the side directly OPPOSITE the leaving group, and the bond to the nucleophile forms as the bond to the leaving group breaks — all in ONE step, with no intermediate. The other three bonds are pushed through to the far side like an umbrella turning inside out, so the configuration is turned over. This is the WALDEN INVERSION.

\(\mathrm{S_N}1\) gives the opposite result. There the leaving group departs first, giving a PLANAR carbocation, which the nucleophile attacks from either face with equal ease — so the product is RACEMIC rather than inverted.

That difference in stereochemistry is one of the main pieces of evidence for the two mechanisms, and observing inversion identifies the bimolecular route as surely as observing racemisation identifies the unimolecular one.

rows.stem: Solubility of gas in liquid decreases with increase in
rows.solution:
Solubility of a gas in a liquid decreases with an increase in TEMPERATURE.

Dissolving a gas is an EXOTHERMIC process — the gas molecules give up kinetic energy and are held by the solvent — so by Le Chatelier's principle warming drives it backwards and less remains in solution.

Equivalently, in \(p = K_{\mathrm{H}}x\), Henry's constant RISES with temperature, and a larger constant means a smaller mole fraction dissolved at any given pressure.

PRESSURE moves it the other way: by Henry's law solubility is directly proportional to the partial pressure, which is why soft drinks are bottled under pressure. Volume and the number of solute molecules are not variables in Henry's law at all.

rows.stem: Which of the following relations is incorrect ?
rows.solution:
The INCORRECT relation is \(\mathrm{G} = \kappa\left(\dfrac{l}{a}\right)\).

Work from the definitions. Resistance is proportional to length and inversely proportional to area:
\(R = \rho\,\dfrac{l}{a} = \dfrac{1}{\kappa}\cdot\dfrac{l}{a}\)
since conductivity \(\kappa\) is the reciprocal of resistivity — so the first relation is correct.

Conductance is the RECIPROCAL of resistance, so it must invert that expression:
\(G = \dfrac{1}{R} = \kappa\,\dfrac{a}{l}\)
which is the second relation, also correct. The option offered inverts the geometric factor and is therefore wrong — it would make a LONGER cell more conducting.

The fourth relation, \(\Lambda_m = \kappa/c\), is the definition of molar conductivity and is correct.

A dimensional check settles it at once: \(\kappa\) carries \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-1}}\), so multiplying by a LENGTH OVER AN AREA (units \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)) gives \(\mathrm{S\ cm^{-2}}\), which is not conductance.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: The reagent that can be used to distinguish acetophenone and benzophenone is
rows.solution:
The reagent is IODINE WITH SODIUM HYDROXIDE — the iodoform test.

Both compounds are aromatic ketones, so most carbonyl reagents cannot separate them. What differs is what sits on the OTHER side of the carbonyl.

ACETOPHENONE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}\), carries a METHYL group there, and a methyl ketone gives the iodoform reaction: a yellow precipitate of \(\mathrm{CHI_3}\) appears.
BENZOPHENONE, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COC_6H_5}\), has a second phenyl group instead and gives none.

The distractors fail because both compounds behave alike towards them. Both are carbonyl compounds, so both give a 2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazone. Neither is an aldehyde, so neither reduces Fehling's solution. And sodium hydrogensulphite adds only to aldehydes and METHYL ketones — which would in fact distinguish them, but it is the less reliable test of the two for aryl ketones.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following compounds will undergo self-condensation in the presence of dilute NaOH solution ?
rows.solution:
PROPANAL, \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CHO}\), undergoes self-condensation.

The aldol reaction begins with the base removing an \(\alpha\)-HYDROGEN — a hydrogen on the carbon NEXT TO the carbonyl — to give a carbanion, which then attacks another molecule's carbonyl carbon. Without an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen there is no carbanion and no reaction.

Propanal's neighbouring carbon is a \(-\mathrm{CH_2}-\) carrying two such hydrogens, so it condenses with itself readily.

The other three have none. \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CHO}\) has a benzene ring on its carbonyl carbon; \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}CHO}\) has a fully substituted carbon there; and \(\mathrm{HCHO}\) has no neighbouring carbon at all.

All three of those undergo the CANNIZZARO reaction with concentrated alkali instead — the route open precisely to aldehydes lacking an \(\alpha\)-hydrogen.

rows.stem: For the reaction \(3\mathrm{A} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{B}\), rate of reaction \(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is equal to
rows.solution:
For \(3\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{B}\),
\(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Build it from the stoichiometry. Each species is divided by its coefficient, the reactant taking a minus sign because it is being consumed:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = +\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

Multiplying through by 3 to isolate the term asked for:
\(-\dfrac{\mathrm{d[A]}}{\mathrm{dt}} = \dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{\mathrm{d[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\)

The physical content is that \(\mathrm{A}\) disappears FASTER than \(\mathrm{B}\) appears — three consumed for every two produced — so the factor must exceed 1. The option with \(2/3\) has the ratio inverted, and it is the right answer to the mirror-image question where the coefficients are swapped.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals shows + 1 and + 2 oxidation states ?
rows.solution:
COPPER shows both \(+1\) and \(+2\).

Copper is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10}4s^1\). Losing the single \(4s\) electron gives \(\mathrm{Cu^+}\), which is \(3d^{10}\) — a completely filled subshell and stable in the solid state. Losing one more gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^9\) and is the state favoured in AQUEOUS solution, because its much larger hydration energy more than repays the second ionisation.

Copper is in fact the only 3d element with a well-established \(+1\) state.

The others cannot. Scandium has only \(+3\); zinc only \(+2\), its \(3d^{10}\) core being untouchable. Manganese runs from \(+2\) to \(+7\) but not \(+1\).

rows.stem: The formula of the complex Iron (III) hexacyanidoferrate (II) is :
rows.solution:
The formula is \(\mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}\).

Read the name in two halves. Iron(III) is the CATION, \(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}\). Hexacyanidoferrate(II) is the complex ANION: six cyanido ligands give \(-6\) against iron at \(+2\), so the ion carries \(2 - 6 = -4\).

Balance the charges. The lowest whole numbers making \(4^-\) and \(3^+\) cancel are three anions and four cations:
\(4 \times (+3) = +12\) and \(3 \times (-4) = -12\)

giving \(\mathrm{Fe_4[Fe(CN)_6]_3}\).

The compound is PRUSSIAN BLUE, and the same iron appears in it in TWO different oxidation states — which is where its intense colour comes from, by charge transfer between them.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : The enthalpy of mixing \(\Delta_{\mathrm{mix}}\mathrm{H}\) is equal to zero for an ideal solution.
Reason (R) : For an ideal solution the interaction between solute and solvent molecules is stronger than the interactions between solute-solute or solvent-solvent molecules.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

For an ideal solution \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H\) IS zero — that is part of what defines one, along with \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}V = 0\) and obedience to Raoult's law over the whole range of composition.

But the Reason describes the wrong situation. In an IDEAL solution the solute-solvent interactions are THE SAME in strength as the solute-solute and solvent-solvent interactions, not stronger.

And that sameness is exactly why the enthalpy change vanishes: heat is absorbed or released only when the new interactions differ from those broken to make room for them, and when all three are alike the energy balances exactly.

STRONGER solute-solvent interactions describe a NEGATIVE deviation from Raoult's law, where mixing is exothermic and \(\Delta_{\text{mix}}H\) is negative — the opposite of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Molar conductivity decreases with increase in concentration.
Reason (R) : When concentration approaches zero, the molar conductivity is known as limiting molar conductivity.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Molar conductivity does decrease as concentration rises, and the limiting molar conductivity is defined as its value when the concentration approaches zero — both statements hold.

But the second merely NAMES a quantity; it does not explain the trend. Calling the extrapolated value \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) tells us what the limit is called, not why the curve slopes as it does.

The actual explanation is about interionic interaction. At higher concentration the ions are closer together and drag on one another, so each moves more slowly than it otherwise would; for a WEAK electrolyte, a higher concentration also means a smaller degree of dissociation. Both effects lower the molar conductivity.

The Reason describes the END POINT of the trend the Assertion states, which is a different thing from its cause.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Transition metals show their highest oxidation state with oxygen.
Reason (R) : The ability of oxygen to form multiple bonds to metals.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Transition metals do reach their highest oxidation states in combination with OXYGEN — manganese at \(+7\) in \(\mathrm{MnO_4^-}\), chromium at \(+6\) in \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\), osmium at \(+8\) in \(\mathrm{OsO_4}\).

The Reason gives the cause exactly. Oxygen has lone pairs available for donation into the metal's empty d orbitals, so an \(\mathrm{M{=}O}\) bond carries \(\pi\) character on top of its \(\sigma\) bond. That extra bonding stabilises a metal in a state it could not otherwise sustain.

FLUORINE is the illuminating comparison. It is MORE electronegative than oxygen, so one might expect it to force still higher states — but it forms only a single \(\sigma\) bond, and manganese's highest fluoride reaches just \(+4\) where its oxide reaches \(+7\). Multiple bonding, not electronegativity, is what does the work.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Chlorobenzene is resistant to nucleophilic substitution reaction at room temperature.
Reason (R) : C-Cl bond gets weaker due to resonance.
rows.context: Given below are two statements labelled as Assertion (A) and Reason (R). Select the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Chlorobenzene does resist nucleophilic substitution at room temperature — its hydrolysis needs about 623 K and 300 atmospheres.

But the Reason reverses the effect of resonance. The chlorine's lone pair is delocalised INTO THE RING, which gives the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond partial DOUBLE BOND character — making it SHORTER and STRONGER, not weaker.

And that is exactly why the Assertion holds: a bond with double bond character does not break to let a nucleophile substitute. Corrected to "stronger", the Reason would have explained the Assertion perfectly; as written it would predict the opposite.

Two further factors point the same way: the carbon carrying the chlorine is \(sp^2\) and holds the shared pair more tightly, and the ring's electron-rich \(\pi\) cloud repels the approaching nucleophile.

rows.stem: What are nucleic acids ? Why two strands in DNA are not identical but are complementary ?
rows.solution:
NUCLEIC ACIDS are biomolecules that are POLYMERS OF NUCLEOTIDES — long chains in which each unit consists of a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group, the phosphate linking one sugar to the next to form the backbone. They are found in the nuclei of living cells, and the two kinds are DNA and RNA.

WHY THE TWO STRANDS ARE COMPLEMENTARY RATHER THAN IDENTICAL. The strands are held together by HYDROGEN BONDS between bases, and those bonds form only between SPECIFIC PAIRS: adenine always with thymine, through two hydrogen bonds, and guanine always with cytosine, through three.

The pairing is fixed by shape and by the arrangement of donor and acceptor atoms — a larger purine must face a smaller pyrimidine for the strands to stay the right distance apart, and only these two combinations align their hydrogen bonds correctly.

So wherever one strand carries adenine, the other MUST carry thymine opposite it. Each strand therefore specifies the other completely — which is exactly what makes replication possible, each strand serving as the template for a new partner.

rows.stem:
Do the following conversions in not more than two steps :
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}\) to \(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3}\) to \(\mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — sub-part (b)'s two compounds are printed only as drawn benzene rings. Both are named losslessly in the stem, so the row is answerable from text, but the drawing is worth showing. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) ETHANOIC ACID TO PROPANONE, in two steps. Count the carbons first: two in, three out, so a carbon must be ADDED — and a dialkylcadmium does that while stopping cleanly at the ketone.

Convert the acid to its acyl chloride:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{SOCl_2}} \mathrm{CH_3COCl}\)

Then treat with dimethylcadmium:
\(\mathrm{CH_3COCl} + (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{Cd} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)

The cadmium reagent is chosen deliberately: it is MILD enough to stop at the ketone, whereas a Grignard reagent would attack the ketone as well and carry on to a tertiary alcohol.

(b) ETHYLBENZENE TO BENZOIC ACID, by drastic oxidation of the side chain. Alkaline permanganate oxidises an alkyl side chain right down to the carboxyl group, whatever its length, and acidification then frees the acid:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2CH_3} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{KMnO_4}/\mathrm{KOH}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOK} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5COOH}\)

Note that the SECOND carbon of the ethyl group is lost entirely — the whole side chain is cut back to a single carboxyl carbon. The ring itself is untouched, benzene rings being resistant to oxidation.
